message.content:
## What visibly improved

The overhead direction is working. Putting the invitation beside the book rather than on a receding page removes the earlier perspective fight, and the hero now reads as one calm composition: dark walnut left, single bright object right. The 2:3 block, tight contact shadow and consistent cover furniture (COLLECTED WRITING / logo / title / subtitle / rule / THE COLLECTED EDITION / 2026) make the four presets genuinely comparable rather than four different layouts. The disclosure copy is much better calibrated — "Cover treatments are proposals for review", "Sample layout; final pagination comes with your proof", "You approve the proof before anything prints" — so nothing here overclaims a wired print path. Mobile (Image 4) reflows sensibly, and the excerpt view (Image 5) is the strongest single frame in the set: real prose, comfortable measure, honest "Excerpt 1 of 3" pagination.

## The three most important remaining faults

**1. The book still reads as a UI rectangle, not a perfect-bound paperback.** The specific missing cues: the four corners are sharp 90° with no radius or fibre; the cover plane is perfectly flat with no gentle cross-cover gradient from the lamp at upper left, so it doesn't take the light the desk does; and the edge treatment is a uniform pale sliver on the right and bottom that reads as a CSS border rather than a stack of 179 pages. Compare Image 6, which despite its problems shows a visible page block and hinge. In the Midnight cover the problem is worst — a dark rectangle with a thin light line looks like a modal, not a printed board. Also, a 6×9 book is 1.5:1, not 2:3 (1.5 exactly — fine), but the spine is entirely absent from every frame, so scale is unreadable: nothing tells the eye whether this is a 34-page pamphlet or a 400-page brick.

**2. Lighting logic is contradictory.** The brass lamp sits top-left and its glow falls on the upper-left wood, yet the contact shadow under the book falls down-right *and* the cover has no directional shading. The shadow is also too small and too even for an object this large — it hugs all four sides equally, which happens under diffuse ambient light, not under a single warm desk lamp. The engraved sheaf, meanwhile, sits in the darkest part of the frame and is barely legible on desktop; on mobile it's cropped into an unreadable smear behind the book at the right edge.

**3. Composition and contrast weak points.** The right column below the book is a long thin stack — tabs, three lines of small caption, a link, a section label, four swatch cards — set in small type on the darkest wood. That caption block ("The publication's own logo and words…") is the lowest-contrast text in the study and deserves real scrutiny even though the automated pass came back clean; the supplied axe result cannot vouch for legibility over a photographic gradient. The four swatch cards are also clipped at the desktop fold, so the "FOUR COVER DIRECTIONS" promise arrives half-visible. On mobile only the selected preset gets a description line, which is fine, but the swatches themselves are too abstract to preview anything.

## Which direction deserves refinement

**Masthead.** It's the only one where the publication, not the print vendor, leads: the logo is big enough to be an identity mark rather than a favicon, the red rule gives the cover an axis, and the heavy sans title survives being reduced to a thumbnail — which matters, since most readers will first meet this at postage-stamp size. It also carries straight through to the excerpt view (Image 5), where the same red rule and small caps CAITHRIN make cover and interior feel like one edition. Classic is competent but generic and its logo is stranded in dead space above an oversized title. Field notes wastes its top third and the fake spine stripe is the least convincing physical cue in the set. Midnight is the most attractive still and the most dangerous: a rich near-black on a printed 6×9 cover will scuff and band, and it invites exactly the foil/cloth expectation you've ruled out.

Note: I can't judge motion, keyboard behaviour, responsiveness beyond these two widths, identity accuracy or print fidelity from stills. Image 6's oblique hero remains unresolved and is a separate artifact.
